Biden-appointed judge deals Trump another sanctuary city defeat in major immigration fight

A federal judge ruled Trump's lawsuit against New York City's sanctuary policies fails, citing the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine.

Actual Article Body:

New York City sanctuary laws are upheld after a federal judge dismisses a Department of Justice lawsuit, drawing sharp criticism from Joe Abraham, whose daughter Katie was killed in a hit-and-run crash. Meanwhile, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul deflects questions on migrant crime during a gubernatorial debate.

A Biden-appointed judge dealt the Trump administration another legal blow Thursday, tossing its lawsuit seeking to upend New York City’s sanctuary policies after ruling that the Justice Department’s arguments amounted to a "backdoor around the Tenth Amendment."

The Trump administration sued New York City in July 2025, alleging that its sanctuary laws unlawfully hinder federal immigration enforcement by restricting local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal authorities.

The New York City case is one of more than two dozen lawsuits the Trump administration has filed against state and local jurisdictions over sanctuary and related policies restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

But U.S. District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr. ruled that the federal government lacked standing to challenge New York City’s restrictions on honoring ICE detainers and rejected the Justice Department’s claims that the city’s sanctuary policies are preempted by federal law.

MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS

Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at Middle Collegiate Church in New York City on March 19, 2026. (Leonardo Munoz/AFP via Getty Images)

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani celebrated the ruling in a Friday post on X, accusing the administration of attempting to turn city employees into immigration enforcement agents.

"The federal government tried to turn our public servants into deportation agents and force New York City to carry out ICE’s cruel agenda. Today, a federal court rejected that effort and upheld our laws. Every New Yorker deserves to seek help from their city without fear of being targeted for deportation. We will stand by our immigrant neighbors, defend our laws and protect the promise that this city belongs to all of us," Mamdani wrote.

Reyes found the administration lacked standing because striking down the city’s restrictions would not remedy its alleged harm because separate state laws restricting cooperation would remain in place.

But Abhishek Kambli, a former federal prosecutor and current partner at Holtzman Vogel, disputed that reasoning, arguing that the city's laws independently harm the federal government's authority regardless of whether similar state restrictions exist.

"The sovereign harm is done just by the fact that New York City has the law in the books, no matter what other factors prevent practical application of the United States's position," Kambli told Fox News Digital.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS

Reyes also rejected the Justice Department's argument that New York City's sanctuary policies are overridden by federal immigration law.

"Even if the United States has standing — and it does not — its preemption claims fail," Reyes wrote. "All of the United States’ preemption claims — express, conflict and field — fail because the relevant federal statutes do not regulate private actors."

Dozens of immigrants are detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents inside the Federal Plaza courthouse in New York City on Thursday, June 26, following their legal proceedings. The arrests, which took place shortly after court appearances, have sparked criticism from immigrant rights advocates, who say courthouse enforcement undermines due process and deters community members from seeking legal protection. (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The judge pointed to the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine, which prevents the federal government from forcing state and local governments to use their own officials and resources to administer federal programs.

"If states cannot remain free to control their agencies and employees to resist federal immigration enforcement, which is within states’ constitutional prerogatives, the Tenth Amendment anticommandeering doctrine means nothing," Reyes wrote.

Kambli, however, argued that Reyes misinterpreted the distinction between forcing local governments to assist federal immigration enforcement and preventing them from actively obstructing it.

"Really what the 10th Amendment anti-commandeering means is you can't force states to go from doing nothing to affirmatively assisting. What these statutes are doing is basically preventing states from actively obstructing federal immigration enforcement," Kambli said.

He argued that the Justice Department was not seeking to force New York City officials to carry out federal immigration enforcement, but instead to prevent local laws from interfering with federal authorities' ability to enforce immigration law.

"That's different from the federal government saying a state or a city is required to actively assist ICE in operations," Kambli said.

President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)

HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE-STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW

The Justice Department also argued that New York City's sanctuary policies went beyond simply refusing to assist federal authorities by restricting information-sharing with ICE that is protected under federal law. The administration additionally claimed that the city unfairly singled out federal immigration officials for restrictions that did not apply to other law enforcement agencies.

Reyes, however, found that federal information-sharing protections apply specifically to information about an individual's citizenship or immigration status and do not require local governments to provide ICE with broader details, such as a person's release date or whereabouts.

"The United States’ assertion that information regarding release dates and custody status is information regarding immigration or citizenship status is contrary to law," Reyes wrote.

Kambli, however, argued that the distinction over what information is being withheld misses the greater issue at hand.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"The issue is mainly whether any state or locality that prohibits cooperation is preempted by federal law, regardless of what the information is," Kambli said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The ruling marks the latest setback for the Trump administration's efforts to challenge sanctuary policies in federal court, following dismissals of similar lawsuits involving Boston, Los Angeles and Minnesota.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Alex Murdaugh judge warns against courtroom ‘circus’ as defense wins DNA fight, loses ballistics bid

LEXINGTON, SC — The judge overseeing Alex Murdaugh’s double-murder retrial rebuked both sides Friday over their bitter evidence fights, warning she “will not allow these proceedings to become a circus.” During the tense hearing, Judge Debra McCaslin handed the defense a win on their DNA testing request but rejected its broader request for ballistic data. ...

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

LEXINGTON, SC — The judge overseeing Alex Murdaugh’s double-murder retrial rebuked both sides Friday over their bitter evidence fights, warning she “will not allow these proceedings to become a circus.”

During the tense hearing, Judge Debra McCaslin handed the defense a win on their DNA testing request but rejected its broader request for ballistic data.

McCaslin also corrected the record on a polygraph claim that Murdaugh attorney Dick Harpootlian made in August, which he said Murdaugh passed with “flying colors.” The judge said Friday that Murdaugh actually failed that test, which was related to his financial crimes, not the murder case.

Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family’s Moselle property in Colleton County.

The South Carolina Supreme Court later overturned the convictions after finding that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced the jury.

His retrial is scheduled to begin April 5, 2027. Murdaugh has maintained his innocence in the killings.

McCaslin sided with the defense over prosecutors’ objections on DNA samples of swabs from Maggie Murdaugh’s phone, even though the analysis will likely consume the last testable samples.

She cited due process and the right to a “full and complete defense.” Murdaugh’s defense team said the testing will likely take about 90 days.

The judge said defense attorneys don’t have to share results of the DNA tests with prosecutors unless they plan to use them at trial.

McCaslin denied Murdaugh’s request for a list of every crime in the 2nd and 14th judicial circuits since 2021 involving .300 Blackout ammunition, for every such firearm recovered, and for casings from other shootings.

She found the theory that the murder weapon is tied to an unsolved crime speculative and was based solely on news reports, adding that the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division doesn’t have a list like that, and a manual review would be too much work and could intrude on investigations that are ongoing.

While the judge denied Harpootlian for his expert to physically test the shell casings from the crime scene, she ordered the state to hand over all raw data to the defense.

She also said prosecutors must hand over 3D crime scene scan data by Monday, but added she won’t make the state produce material several times and asked the defense to have staff sign for discovery.

McCaslin issued a similar warning when the state agreed to provide the defense with cellphone extraction data from Maggie and Paul’s phone, but said this would be the last time the state will hand it over.

To close the hearing, McCaslin granted a state motion to correct the record regarding Harpootlian’s assertion at an Aug. 14 hearing that Murdaugh had passed a polygraph “with flying colors.”

She said Murdaugh had been administered a polygraph concerning whether he concealed other assets and failed it, and that he has never taken a polygraph related to the killings of Maggie and Paul Murdaugh.

McCaslin acknowledged that Harpootlian had submitted a letter expressing apology for any confusion, then cautioned both sides that “candor with the court is not optional.”

McCaslin also ruled in prosecutors’ favor on a defense motion requesting evidence related to the disposal of the murder weapons, which have never been recovered.

McCaslin said the state is required to hand over the material only if it proves favorable to Murdaugh’s defense.

Murdaugh’s defense team initially asked the judge to force prosecutors to turn over information it has “concerning the handling, transport, concealment, or disposal of the alleged weapons used to kill Maggie Murdaugh and Paul Murdaugh, including the statement a witness gave to agents of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division in 2023 that a Lowcountry police chief spoke of arriving early at the scene and of providing Defendant Murdaugh a change of clothes, the reports of every interview conducted on that subject, and the testimony and exhibits presented to the State Grand Jury concerning it.”

According to the motion, filed in late September by Murdaugh’s attorneys, press reports indicate that a state grand jury received testimony alleging Yemassee Police Chief Greg Alexander was observed in possession of the murder weapons shortly after the June 7, 2021, killings.

“According to those reports, witnesses have testified that the Chief of Police of the Town of Yemassee, Greg Alexander, was seen with the murder weapons in the immediate aftermath of the June 7, 2021, killings, and that second Yemassee officer is under investigation for transporting and concealing weapons and clothing,” the filing states.

It cites a story from The Post and Courier, which reported that “a Lowcountry official told SLED agents that Chief Alexander ‘spoke of arriving early to the murder scene and talked about providing a change of clothes to Murdaugh,’ and that the official believed the guns and clothing were brought into the police station and stored there.”

Notably, the allegations couldn’t be corroborated by The Post and Courier.

Alexander, through his attorney, Joe McCulloch, denied accusations made in the media reports.

“The same explanation has been provided to SLED,” McCulloch told Fox News Digital. “That truth will outlive any ridiculous rumors and gossip.”

Former prosecutor Joshua Ritter told Fox News Digital he considers the allegation against Alexander a “wild goose chase.”

“This is one of those cases that, you know, a lot of reporting was done early on, a lot of conspiracy theories swirling around this case,” Ritter said.

“I don’t see any reason for the judge to allow for this essentially wild goose chase in regards to an uncorroborated report about law enforcement perhaps being in possession of the murder weapon.”

“Obviously, the defense would love to pursue this to its absolute limit because they think that there’s a snowball’s chance that it might yield something, but I think that the judge is probably going to give very little leeway on something like this,” he added.
